source.title: Can the capability of Large Language Models be described by human ability? A Meta Study
source.authors: Ming-Rui Zan; Yun-Quan Zhang; Bo-Yang Zhang; Fang-Min Liu; Da-Ning Cheng

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al.'s scaling laws to motivate considering parameter scale, but it does not measure pretraining loss, tokens, or compute, fit scaling curves, or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper analyzes benchmark-score rankings and how their clusters differ between parameter-size groups. Those results do not test the loss scaling, extrapolation, architecture, modality, downstream predictability, or fit-dependence claims stated here. The paper's own scale-group comparison is recorded as a related finding under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to justify restricting analysis to models under 10B parameters. It clusters benchmark rank correlations within size groups. It reports no loss, no power-law fit, and no relation between scale or loss and downstream score, so it neither tests nor uses the scaling-law finding as a tool. Relation is cites_only (T6), not uses_without_test (T4).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude three things: some capabilities of <10B LLMs can be described by human-ability categories; abilities that are related in humans can be nearly uncorrelated in LLMs; and which capabilities appear stable changes with parameter scale, with some emerging and others dissipating.
record.recipe_differences: This is a meta-study of benchmark rankings and capability clusters, not a reproduction or application of the original scaling-law fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis compares parameter-size groups; it uses average-linkage hierarchical clustering and reports that other linkage methods did not produce fundamentally different outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Benchmark rank-correlation cluster structure differs between the <10B and 10–20B model groups. The largest cluster is 24 benchmarks for <10B and up to 34 for 10–20B. Knowledge benchmarks merge and understanding benchmarks split in the larger group.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Correlation structure among LLM benchmark rankings changes with parameter-size group.

record.problems: The paper states that the number of ultra-large models is small and that stable ranking-based analysis above 20 billion parameters is difficult. It does not report uncertainty estimates for the cluster findings. Its results concern rankings and clusters rather than losses or scaling-law fits.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured or fitted.
No other modality or training regime.
No downstream score is related to parameter count or loss; analysis is rank correlations within size bins.
No exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation and tranche guesses (uses_without_test, T4) are changed to cites_only (T6). The Kaplan citation only motivates binning by size; the paper's method does not rely on any scaling result. The comparison across size groups is uncontrolled: the groups have different model counts (52 vs 30), and the benchmark count is inconsistent (37 benchmarks overall, 52 cited for 10–20B). No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation or loss-minimising parameter/token split is studied.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
No scaling-law test in other modalities or training regimes is reported.
The paper does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss; it clusters benchmark rankings within parameter-size groups.
No scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending are examined.

rows.subject: LLMs with fewer than 10B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Clustered benchmark-score rankings using Spearman correlation and hierarchical clustering.
rows.measure: Largest cluster size in the benchmark-ranking clustering
rows.note: Aggregate result for the parameter-size group; the paper does not specify what the cluster samples represent in this sentence or relate the cluster size to a loss-scaling prediction.
rows.check: This is a cluster-size statistic of benchmark rank correlations (24 benchmarks in the largest cluster, <10B group). It is not a loss or downstream-performance measure, so it is correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: LLMs with parameter sizes between 10 and 20 billion
rows.operation_detail: Clustered benchmark-score rankings using Spearman correlation and hierarchical clustering.
rows.measure: Largest cluster size in the benchmark-ranking clustering
rows.baseline: The largest cluster for models with fewer than 10B parameters comprised 24 samples
rows.note: Aggregate result for the parameter-size group. The authors also state that knowledge-application benchmarks clustered together in this group, while the understanding cluster seen for smaller models did not remain cohesive.
rows.check: This is a cluster-size statistic (up to 34 benchmarks, 10–20B group). It is not a performance-versus-scale measure. The baseline is r1's value from a different group with a different benchmark count (the text says 52 benchmarks for 10–20B versus 37 overall), so the two cluster sizes are not directly comparable.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
